essentialQuestion.source: How can we tell reliable information from misleading information?
essentialQuestion.back: How can you tell trustworthy information from misleading information?

read.sections.0.heading.source: Loud is not the same as true

read.sections.0.text.note: 'claim' = 'nhận định' (KEY_TERMS). 'nhận định' can sound like 'assessment/judgement' in everyday Vietnamese; alternatives 'khẳng định', 'tuyên bố'. 'source' = 'nguồn'. 'honest mistakes' as 'nhầm lẫn không cố ý'. | Review: 'viết toàn chữ in hoa' (written entirely in capitals) is a touch stronger than English 'with capital letters'; acceptable for the 'shouting' example.
read.sections.0.text.source: Messages spread very fast on phones and messaging apps. Some are true, some are honest mistakes and some are completely invented. A message with capital letters that says “Share now” can feel urgent, but that does not make it true. To judge any claim, first identify its source. Post A has no name, no date and no link, so nobody can tell where it really came from. Post B is a signed notice on the centre's own page, and it is dated today. It also gives evidence: exact times and a clear reason for the closure. A clear source with specific details is usually more trustworthy.
read.sections.0.text.back: Messages spread very fast on phones and messaging apps. Some are true, some are unintentional mistakes and some are made up completely. A message written entirely in capital letters that says "Share now" can make us feel hurried, but that does not make it true. To judge any claim, first you need to know its source. Post A has no name, no date and no link, so no one knows where it really comes from. Post B is a signed notice on the centre's own page, and shows today's date. It also gives evidence: specific times and a clear reason for the closing. A clear source together with specific details is usually more trustworthy.

read.sections.0.simpler.note: Longest sentence 18 syllables, kept for the meaning. Check it is natural.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: Messages move fast on phones. Some are true. Some are wrong. A post in big letters that says “Share now” can feel important. But that does not make it true. When you see a claim, ask about the source. Who made it? Post A has no name and no date. Post B comes from the centre itself. It has a date. It also has evidence, like exact times. So Post B is easier to trust.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Messages spread fast on phones. Some are true. Some are false. A post written in capital letters saying "Share now" can make us feel it is important. But that does not make it true. When you see a claim, ask about the source. Who made it? Post A has no name and no date. Post B comes from the centre itself. It has a date. It also has evidence, like specific times. So Post B is easier to believe.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Check the date and the context

read.sections.1.text.note: 'bối cảnh' for context (KEY_TERMS). 'do máy tính tạo ra' for 'made by a computer' (AI-generated images are not named in the English).
read.sections.1.text.source: Even a real photo can mislead people. Post C shows a real locked door, but the photo is from last year, so it cannot tell us anything about tomorrow. The date, the place and the reason for a photo are its context, and context changes what a photo means. Photos can also be edited with apps, or even made by a computer. The giant fish in Message F looks strange at the edges, and nobody else has a picture of it. When a photo or story seems surprising, look for the same news from another trusted source.
read.sections.1.text.back: Even a real photo can deceive people. Post C shows a real locked door, but the photo was taken last year, so it tells us nothing about tomorrow. The date, place and reason a photo was taken are its context, and context changes the meaning of the photo. Photos can also be edited with an app, or even made by a computer. The giant fish in Message F has a strange-looking edge, and no one else has a photo of it. When a photo or a story seems surprising, look for the same news from another trustworthy source.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A real photo can still trick you. Post C shows a real door. But the photo is from last year. It does not show tomorrow. When and where a photo was taken is its context. Context can change what a photo means. Some photos are changed with apps. Some are made by computers. The big fish in Message F looks strange. No one else has a photo of it. Look for the news in another place you trust.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A real photo can still deceive you. Post C has a real door. But the photo was taken last year. It does not show tomorrow. When and where the photo was taken is its context. Context can change the meaning of the photo. Some photos are edited with an app. Some photos are made by a computer. The big fish in Message F looks strange. No one else has a photo of it. Look for that news in another place that you trust.

read.sections.2.text.note: 'tin đồn' (rumour), 'kiểm chứng' (verify) per KEY_TERMS. The sentence 'Hãy hỏi ba câu: ...' keeps the three questions exactly.
read.sections.2.text.source: A rumour is a story that spreads from person to person without proof. Message D and Message E are both like rumours. Message D does not explain who is giving away the free boots. Message E says “doctors don't want you to know”, but it names no doctor or health organisation. Before sharing any message, try to verify it. Ask three questions: Who made it? When was it made? What is the evidence? Then compare it with a trusted source, such as a teacher, a health worker or an official notice. If you cannot verify a message, it is usually safer not to forward it.
read.sections.2.text.back: A rumour is a story that spreads from person to person without evidence. Message D and Message E both look like rumours. Message D does not explain who is giving free boots. Message E says "doctors don't want you to know", but does not name any doctor or health organisation. Before sharing any message, try to verify it. Ask three questions: Who made it? When was it made? What is the evidence? Then compare with a trustworthy source, like a teacher, a health worker or an official notice. If you cannot verify a message, it is usually safer not to forward it.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: A rumour is a story that spreads with no proof. Messages D and E are like rumours. They do not say who made them. Before you share, try to verify the message. Ask: Who made it? When? What is the evidence? Then ask someone you trust, like a teacher or a health worker. If you cannot check it, do not send it on.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: A rumour is a story that spreads without evidence. Messages D and E look like rumours. They do not say who made them. Before sharing, try to verify the message. Ask: Who made it? When? What is the evidence? Then ask a person you trust, like a teacher or a health worker. If you cannot check it, do not send it on.

watch.why.back: The video explains how facts, opinions and mistakes get into the news, and how a careful reader can tell them apart.

watch.summary.note: Video tips translated closely. 'think/likely/probably' as 'nghĩ rằng / có khả năng / có lẽ'. Check the three hedge words are the usual ones in news Vietnamese. | Review: Five consecutive sentences start with 'Hãy' when read aloud; meaning is exact, a native speaker may want to vary. Also 'đừng kiểm tra cứ vài phút một lần' keeps the English's ambiguity about what is checked.
watch.summary.source: This animated video is about how to choose your news. Not long ago, most people got news from a few newspapers and TV channels. Now the internet brings much more news, from many more people. Different sources may even disagree about the facts. The video gives some tips. When you can, find the first source, like the real report or speech. When a big story is still happening, do not check every few minutes. Wait for clear facts. Read the same story in more than one place. Look for words like “think”, “likely” or “probably”. They show that a report is not sure. Be careful when a report does not say who gave the facts. Most important, check a story before you share it.
watch.summary.back: This animated video is about how to choose your own news. Not long ago, most people got news from a few newspapers and TV channels. Now the internet brings much more news, from many more people. Different sources may even disagree with each other about the facts. The video gives a few tips. When you can, look for the first source, like the real report or speech. When a big event is still going on, do not check every few minutes. Wait for clear facts. Read the same story in more than one place. Look for words like "think that", "likely" or "perhaps". They show the report is not certain. Be careful when a report does not say who gave the facts. Most important, check a story before you share it.
